This was a childhood favorite for me so it was kind of a hard watch looking past the rose-tinted glasses as not only an older viewer, but also as someone who does still deeply love classic Simpsons. The jokes that I remember still hit today, but a lot were trying to land off the idea of finding Homer’s horrible personality in this movie to be funny. It just wasn’t. In the way that The Spongebob Movie is often referred to as the last piece of good classic Spongebob, I feel The Simpsons Movie is a weird science experiment of classic Simpsons and modern Simpsons comedy that blends together in a strange new form that doesn’t work for me as it once did as a child who just saw “The Funny Yellow Family”. There are remnants of what made The Simpsons so good for me even today here. Theres pieces of genuine heartfelt moments that you’d find in the golden era, but you have to trudge through the off characterization and unfunny jokes that Homer is just the worst but will eventually be forgiven because he’s the main man. Why yes, I CAN believe this had 11 freaking writers, because this feels like 11 different people’s view as to what the Simpsons are, and none of them mesh in a way that makes more than four moments of this any good. Like, it’s weird how much this feels like Simpsons fanfic, despite being done by 11 separate showrunners; these are all people who know Springfield pretty intimately, and so it’s extra heartbreaking that they managed to make something that feels more like A Very Special Episode of the show than anything the show has ever done. And yes, I get that they had to shoehorn a decades-long show into 90 minutes, but making this weirdly serious — separation! parental drama! Unresolved mystery! — feels like a colossal miscalculation and a betrayal of everything the Simpsons are so that they can make this feel justified as a movie. Worse, it feels like they don’t even get the characters. For example, Homer is just the dumbest, most random, most insufferable version of himself that’s ever existed, and there’s almost no line here that feels organic; it’s all [INSERT HOMER SAYING SOMETHING AGGRESSIVELY RANDOM AND UNKNOWINGLY HARMFUL] over and over, and there’s no effort to tie it into explanations as to why he’s suddenly just like this evil random gas leak version of himself. Again, I found maybe three or four of the gags to be kinda funny, and they all feel like Monorail-era level of quality. The rest feel like “ha ha we showed Bart’s dong” or “ha ha Homer flips the bird” or just oddly disconnected beats too lazy to be any good. This was a huge bummer even if it did give us the meme-era gold of “this was the worst day of your life SO FAR.” The rest? Oof.

I was selected to lead, not to read Last Watch: September 2020 Age: 51 (at time of release) Source: Disney+ 2026 Challenge: Hanks at 70 Film: #38 Director/Cast/Premise The Simpsons Movie is the 2007 animated comedy directed by David Silverman. Starring Dan Castellaneta, Nancy Cartwright and Tom Hanks the plot sees the residents of Springfield imprisoned under a glass dome. Original Thoughts 2020 Things have a habit of following trends. When your career starts to develop as an actor you get more involved in the production of films, maybe set up your own company. If you have a tv show that becomes popular you end up making a film version. South Park did it in 1999, The Simpsons did it in 2007, is it necessary? No. Was the Simpsons movie worth it? Not really. The reality is that the film was a huge financial success but suffers from a number of expected problems; there are clear pacing issues that is most likely due to the inexperience of putting out anything beyond a normal episode run time, plenty of padding which is often dull and the material/character arcs that offer nothing new from its hundreds of available episodes with far too few jokes. There is a clear over reliance of the audiences fondness for the characters. Its these viewers who paid to watch an extended version of an episode and who the studio banked on making this a success. What you get is familiarity of the Springfield setting and Simpsons regulars with the odd cameo (Tom Hanks included) and sharper animation. For good measure they throw in some themes of religion and the environment whilst ripping off Stephen Kings Under the Dome. Oh and throw in a pig...it just isn't worth it.

Just like The Simpsons, this review series has been running too long. I LOVE The Simpsons. The show has really shaped humor and culture for hundreds and hundreds of people. The show’s peak was from seasons 2-8, from 1991 to 1997. So, dear reader, you might be asking along with me: why the hell did they wait until 2007, far past when people had been saying the show had been running too long, to make The Simpsons Movie? Who the hell knows, but it really is a detriment. While the think the film definitely has its very funny moments, it lacks a lot of the intelligence, both in the humor and emotion, that the show had. The film feels like a long version of a Simpsons episode, which really doesn’t work. I think that even if you’ve never written anything in your life, the structure of a 22 minute episode is far different from the structure of a 90 minute movie. I think a lot of movies based off shows have that issue, such as The South Park Movie, but that film worked much better for a few reasons. 1. The humor in The South Park Movie was consistently gutbustingly hilarious, whereas in The Simpsons Movies, while there aren’t any stinker jokes, the majority of them are just ok. There aren’t a lot of jokes I’ll be quoting over and over all watching it. 2. The South Park movie actually plays out like a film, the story is coherent, emotional beats pay off, running jokes resolve, and you feel like you actually watched something of cinematic scale. The Simpsons movie feels a lot looser, like a TV episode, but that means that plot lines don’t make sense, or don’t resolve, the emotional bits don’t really work out, and it overall feels less cinematic. 3. The South Park Movie did something above and beyond the show. The film had a massive scale, a lot of the animation was upped, and there were a bunch of over the top Broadway style musical numbers, stuff you wouldn’t see on a typical South Park episode. The Simpsons Movie feels like an episode of The Simpsons, even down to the animation. There is very little to distinguish the film from an episode. Homer’s opening joke of “why do we pay to watch something we get on TV for free” really feels indicative of the film’s quality. Overall, not really a bad film, but not really a must watch. Definitely only recommend it for hardcore fans.

Llevar una de las comedias más influyentes de la historia de la televisión a la gran pantalla era una maniobra inevitable, pero cargada de riesgos. Estrenada tras años de especulaciones y en un punto donde la serie de televisión ya mostraba signos claros de desgaste creativo, Los Simpson: La película asumió el reto de transformar una dinámica televisiva de 22 minutos en un evento cinematográfico de escala global. El resultado es un largometraje sumamente entretenido, vistoso y con picos cómicos altísimos, aunque empañado por decisiones narrativas que se alejan de la esencia más pura de Springfield. El apartado visual es, sin lugar a dudas, uno de sus puntos más sólidos. La transición hacia un dibujo más estilizado, apoyado por sombreados digitales y una paleta de colores vibrante, le otorgó al largometraje la escala de evento que exigía el cine. La dirección aprovecha las dimensiones de la pantalla grande para desplegar secuencias mucho más dinámicas —como la construcción de la cúpula sobre Springfield o el escape de la familia—, respaldadas por una banda sonora de John Powell que eleva la tensión sin perder la ironía característica de la franquicia. Sin embargo, el núcleo de la historia tropieza en la definición de sus prioridades. El conflicto central opta por apoyarse de forma casi exclusiva en una crisis matrimonial entre Homero y Marge, una fórmula narrativa ampliamente explotada en la serie que aquí se percibe cargada de clichés románticos. La decisión de volcar la carga emotiva en el reencuentro de la pareja le resta espacio al desarrollo de otras dinámicas de la ciudad y fuerza un todo sentimental que por momentos se siente ajeno a la acidez satírica que convirtió a la serie en un fenómeno cultural. A esto se suma una caracterización de Homero que no termina de asentarse. Si bien cuenta con momentos memorables dentro del metraje, se extrañan aquellos rasgos de su personalidad que construyeron sus mejores épocas en televisión: esa mezcla única entre tontería entrañable, momentos de astucia involuntaria y una relación más auténtica con sus vecinos y su entorno. En la película, gran parte de sus acciones quedan subordinadas a empujar el conflicto romántico, dejando en segundo plano su faceta como catalizador del caos social de Springfield. Los Simpson: La película funciona muy bien como pieza de entretenimiento rápido y cumple con el cometido de reunir a generaciones frente a la pantalla. Posee un ritmo ágil y chistes que han quedado grabados en la cultura popular, pero al balancear los elementos, queda la sensación de que prefirió ir a lo seguro antes que arriesgarse a construir un relato verdaderamente memorable. Un hito visual y nostálgico que aprueba con solvencia, pero que se queda lejos del brillo de los mejores años de la familia amarilla. Una entrega entretenida y técnicamente impecable que cumple con el espectáculo visual que exige la gran pantalla. Sin embargo, su dependencia de un conflicto romántico trillado y la pérdida de matices clave en Homero le impiden alcanzar el nivel de los mejores capítulos de la serie.

As a movie, this is a very agreeable watch. It’s never boring and moves at a brisk and consistently amusing 87 minutes. There are also some laugh-out-loud funny lines and moments that are memorable on their own outside of the film’s rather unmemorable context. “Worst day of your life so far ” is remembered as one of the best of the best Homer Simpson quotes, and rightly so. This is a decent time-waster that doesn’t make you feel like you’ve wasted your time once the end credits start to roll. Inoffensive, not great, but not terrible either, and it gets the job done overall. For a major release PG-13 comedy from 2007, you could do infinitely worse. As a Simpsons movie, this sucks very hard for all of the same reasons that make it an okay regular movie. Yes, we were well past the point of the show’s historic Golden Age™️ at the time of this film’s original release, and I don’t know that a better movie than the one we got here could have been realistically expected. I don’t think this movie deserves a pass for that, though. Regardless of the condition The Simpsons TV series was in at the time, or before, or after, there’s no good reason not to expect The Simpsons Movie to be one of the funniest and most iconic comedies of all time, considering the source material. In fact, one of the best comedies in the history of cinema is kind of the bare minimum for which anything calling itself The Simpsons Movie should strive. To see something as irreverent, inventive and ambitious as The Simpsons , the best and most important thing to ever happen on TV (sorry, Moon Landing, if that is your real name…) play things so safe, sanitized and watered down for their long overdue feature film debut is…disappointing, to say the least. To say more than that: it’s not just that this is really weak for a Simpsons movie, but it’s genuinely upsetting to me on an existential level that this is a Simpsons movie, which is a strange feeling to have towards a movie I largely like watching in the moment. However, it always evaporates from my memory almost immediately after the end credits kick in, and all of the negativity and criticism comes flooding back in like clockwork. Eventually the anger subsides, and I’m just left feeling empty and bummed out about the whole thing. Conversely, IF FOUND, PLEASE RETURN TO HOMER J. SIMPSON (NO REWARD) still gets me to laugh like an idiot every time. 5 out of 10 BORT license plates, and deliberately not inviting Bill Oakley and Josh Weinstein to work on the screenplay with all of the other show-runners & legacy writers was a major dick move.

Having premiered nearly forty years ago, The Simpsons is one of the longest last series airing on television.  However you may feel about its quality as it progresses, it is a testament to how popular it is that it has lasted as long as it has.  Of course, given said popularity, it was inevitable that movie starring the residents of Springfield would come to fruition.  When it comes to series being adapted to film, The Simpsons Movie is not among the worst of its kind and is entertaining.  However, it does come with a few of its own drawbacks. The Simpsons Movie goes for a grander plotline that is more fitting for a ninety minute feature than a half hour special.  This time, it is a series of careless accidents brought upon by Homer Simpson that brings great danger to Springfield.  Homer has been known for getting into trouble because of his stupidity or outright selfishness but it's a whole town that's at stake because of his flaws as opposed to matters with family or close friends.  It is a plot that does fit in with what the series was about, even having some clever political jokes here and there. Where the film does suffer a little is that, even with the more epic storyline, it also feels like an extended episode of the show.  This might hit a little differently for people who watch the show religiously while newcomers may be confused.  There are a few laughs to be found from fourth wall jokes and innuendos (some of which would have been censored on the actual show) but it also feels like it's fan service.  It's especially evident when random recurring characters pop up to do what the audience expects without really contributing too much to the actual plot.  Furthermore, the moments that are meant to feel emotional feel a little too quick to make way for some more jokes and action set pieces. The animation of the film keeps true to that of the show along with Matt Groening's own style.  It has been clearly been upgraded for a cinematic outing as it adds more shading and color, reflecting the higher budget.  At times it is even more fluid, partially a result of some former Disney animators having a hand in the making of it (There are a couple of humorous jokes at their expense as well).  It's a style that may not appeal to everyone, but fans of the show should be pleased that it doesn't go for something completely different on a technical level. All the original cast members return to voice their respective characters.  Dan Castellaneta does manage to capture Homer's dimwitted nature.  It is a little hard to get behind the character at times due to how emotionally distant he is for much of the film but Castellaneta is still having fun.  Julie Kavner gets more of a chance to show some range as Marge Simpson.  Bart feels a bit more short changed as he does have a potentially compelling plot but it's not given enough development though Nancy Cartwright still brings her A-game.  Albert Brooks is entertaining as a newcomer, the villainous Russ Cargill, who takes advantage of Homer's accidents in order to destroy Springfield. The Simpsons Movie is a mostly humorous, if slight adaptation of the series.  Much of the time it does feel like it is pandering to fans or stretching out a story way too thin.  Still, its entertainment value lies on its production, the voice acting and some clever writing and jokes.  It is one of the more decent theatrical adaptations of an animated TV show.

It's fine, as the potential finale to the show it's pretty good so the fact it went on for 20 more years(!) isn't a deduction in retrospect. It has the TV-to-movie problem of it being a comedy but requiring high stakes to justify its existence and the runtime. It is obviously a funny concept, and some jokes are a bit darker than the show (I'd forgotten they wanted to lynch Maggie - crazy they all moved past it) but the marriage crisis doesn't work for me in a Simpsons comedy. I think maybe because the soul-searching part never clicked with me, but also, it factually kills the vibe. It's a great character dynamic and is a high stake, but is that what we want from a comedy? Maybe it's just not a comedy style that works outside of a runtime crunch as they did in the golden age. Checking out the deleted scenes for the first time, there is a recency bias, but I wish they were left in. While on the surface, this film feels like a continuation of the extremely long running beloved animated series, it really is a deeply complex insight into the world of a (almost) nuclear family on the brink of destruction due to an emotionally absent father. When considering that this movie came out in 2007 at the height of the 5th Harry Potter film, Spider-Man 3, and the newest Pirates of the Caribbean, this movie, often flies under the radar for being one of the most insightful movies of the year. However, this doesn’t mean that its impact is any less important. While, it didn’t break any records in the box office it’s still manages to give an extremely nuanced view at the detriment behind what will occur when somebody chooses themselves over their loved ones. Homer in this showcases his duality by stepping into the antagonist role by being a character that just can’t seems to stop screwing up. As a result of this, he ends up, turning his entire family and friends against him and as audience members we get to watch him deal with the isolation involved with destroying the structured comfortability associated with familial ties. This is an extremely refreshing take on the series since often cheap jokes are written off to excuse Homer for his genuinely awful behavior. This movie does something smart by allowing the audience to see how Homer’s actions towards his family create turmoil to the point of Marge literally stealing the kids to take them away from the situation Homer has caused. This film is not only a masterclass in the human condition, but it also showcases how regardless of how terrible of a person homer is he still like every human deserves forgiveness. It’s sort of a beautiful story wrapped up in a 90 minute runtime that had me laughing as hard as I did the first time I watched it. Also, it has spider pig and he’s awesome.

I think one of the reasons this works so well for me is the timelessness of the comedy, you could put this movie in theaters today and change nothing and it'd still be a hit, something that can't be said for many many comedies. Besides aging wonderfully comedically, the story here is exactly what I personally love for theatrical TV movies. There's a plot that warrants a longer runtime yet still space for small bits and antics that make it feel like I'm still watching an episode. This might sound insane but I really cannot stand it when a TV show gets a theatrical release and it feels like I'm watching TV characters in a movie not  a longer higher budget episode. Examples of ones I like are this obviously, the Bob's Burgers movie, Mask of the Phantasm, Cowboy Bebop and ofc like the Demon Slayer, JJK, AOT movies, versus things like the Fullmetal Alchemist movies that feel like transplanted characters in a plot and lowkey detracts from the overall narrative. Anyways off that tangent I really really wish they stuck with emotional beat of Marge leaving Homer a little bit longer, because as thousands of people have said that's by far the strongest moment of the whole film. The animation was something I appreciated as well, swinging the camera around and using perspective in ways you don't see in episodes. All around I had a great time, I'm sad I got banned from watching the Simpsons and didn't get to watch this growing up
